[b][u]Interview of Simon Akpan, LMRN broadcast, March 29th, 2007[/u][/b]

[spoiler]So, [i]the interviewer named Shana asks,[/i] What happened after the revolutionaries occupied the town and armory? [i]The camera pans to an old man dressed in a simple outfit of a white dress shirt and tan pants, accompanied by a sun hat.[/i] Well, after a week or two they started dropping leaflets from some old two engine aircraft I can only assume was the only thing that had a bay and wasnt some imposing bomber bristling with guns. Me and the other kids would stop and stare at it as it passed over the town a few times every other day, dropping leaflets and showing off its green belly and the orange triangles on the wings. [i]Hearing this, the interviewer pulls out a printed photograph, the same image displaying on the screen saying Jarisa SB-1, 234 units produced from 1936-1939, and the aircraft is almost exactly as described by the man.[/i] Did it look like this? [i]The man takes a long look at it and nods.[/i] This to a tee. It would drop leaflets telling us to evacuate, but only half of the people went to seek shelter elsewhere. Too many people were sentimental or simply found it too dangerous to travel to other towns nearby, but that was a mistake.

[i]The interviewer shifts in her seat, seemingly uncomfortable knowing what he will tell her about next.[/i] They stopped after three weeks, seemingly giving up on warning us. Not like those who stayed would have listened to more leaflets anyway, and there were more revolutionaries replacing the population who left. Maybe it made us a bigger target with all the buildup, but I dont think they changed plans anyhow. I remember the day of the bombing very well. It was July 17th, 1963, a very hot day as to be expected in the desert, however the shore did bring some respite for us when we had freetime. I was on the beach with my siblings when the dots just above the horizon appeared. Only I noticed them, but thought nothing of it, but the revolutionaries surely did. They powered up their makeshift air-raid alarm and our mother quickly brought us in from the beach and told us to grab whatever we could carry. My grandfathers wisdom must have been stuck in her mind because she grabbed as much food and water as possible and had us take cover in an old gold mine on the side of the mountain which overlooked our town.

[i]The man sighs and continues.[/i] Thats when the engines became audible. The lumbering formation got closer and closer till they broke off into two parts no more than 15 miles from the beach. They sent one over the town, seemingly the gauge of the air defense. The revolutionaries shot at it of course. Only the few machine guns they had seemed to draw any attention from the aircraft as they prompted it to maneuver. I guess they eventually hit it or it had done its job, because it broke off from its turn and sprinted back into the horizon. That prompted the first wave. Six of those large planes dove down on the town, releasing a stream of bullets with the sound that can only be compared to a motorcycle stuck in high gear. Their many guns targeted those in the streets and on trucks, gunning down many who were still running for shelter and managing to destroy two of the machine guns firing back at them. This was simply the softening though.

[i]The screen zooms out as he talks and plays black and white footage taken during the attack by a soldier just outside the town. The grainy film shows planes making passes on the town and tracers streaming down onto whatever targets they deemed dangerous, including a fuel storage tank causing a large plume of smoke to rise in the background.[/i]

After they had emptied their guns, the second wave came. They didnt dive, they simply kept their path and overflew the town, dropping things that tumbled like a poorly thrown rock. The second these containers hit the ground they burst into a great firestorm, enveloping almost the entire town. I saw a few people run into the river that ran parallel to the main road, on fire and plunging themselves into the water in hopes to stop the burning. One vehicle of the revolutionaries, a small car that was owned by a soldier who my older sister had been seeing, escaped the inferno and took off on the road to another town. They wouldnt allow that though. One of the circling planes from the first wave dove on the car, unleashed a burst of what I assume were cannon rounds into the car. It veered off the road and flipped, throwing half a man out of it and onto the road. They circled for perhaps another ten minutes and then left back into the horizon, leaving an apocalyptic scene in their wake. [i]Yet again the film on screen corroborates his telling, even capturing the aftermath of the car.[/i]

[i]Suddenly, the recording of the interview is interrupted by an ad break, and before the announcer can get a word out, the recording ends.[/i][/spoiler]
